title: Birth, Life and Death of Stars
summary: How stars form in nebulae, how they produce energy by nuclear fusion, the life cycles of average and massive stars, and the sun's place among the stars.

notes.text: Stars are born in **nebulae**: huge clouds of gas (mostly hydrogen) and dust in space. Gravity pulls parts of the cloud together. As the cloud collapses it spins and heats up, forming a **protostar**. When the core becomes hot enough (about 15 million °C), **nuclear fusion** begins and a star is born.
The process in which the nuclei of light atoms (hydrogen) join to form heavier atoms (helium), releasing enormous amounts of energy as light and heat.

For most of its life a star is a **main sequence star**, steadily fusing hydrogen into helium. Two forces are balanced: **gravity** pulls the star inwards, and the **outward pressure** from the energy released by fusion pushes outwards. The sun is a main sequence star about 4,6 billion years old, roughly halfway through its life.

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: The more massive a star, the hotter and brighter it burns and the **shorter** its life. Massive stars use up their hydrogen in a few million years; the sun will last about 10 billion years; small red dwarfs may last trillions of years.

notes.caption: Life cycles
headers: Massive star (more than about 8 times the sun's mass)
rows: Red giant: hydrogen runs out, the outer layers swell and cool
Planetary nebula: outer layers drift away as a glowing shell
Supernova: a massive explosion, brighter than a whole galaxy for a short time
White dwarf: a small, hot, dense core that slowly cools

notes.text: A region in space where matter is so tightly packed that its gravity is strong enough to stop even light from escaping.
The extremely dense remaining core of a supernova; a teaspoon of it would weigh billions of tonnes.
In about 5 billion years the sun will become a **red giant**, swallowing Mercury and Venus and possibly Earth, before ending as a **white dwarf**.

notes.title: What will happen to this star?
notes.problem: Describe the end of (a) a star like the sun and (b) a star many times more massive.
steps: (a) A sun-like star swells into a **red giant**, sheds its outer layers and leaves a **white dwarf**.
(b) A very massive star becomes a **supergiant** and explodes in a **supernova**.
What is left is a neutron star or, for the most massive stars, a black hole.
notes.answer: (a) White dwarf. (b) Supernova, then a neutron star or black hole.

notes.text: We are made of star stuff

The early universe contained mostly hydrogen and helium. Heavier elements such as carbon, oxygen and iron were made by fusion inside stars, and elements heavier than iron (like gold) were made in supernova explosions. When stars die they scatter these elements into space, where they form new stars, planets and eventually living things.

notes.title: Reading a star's colour
notes.problem: Rigel looks blue-white and Betelgeuse looks red. Which is hotter? Where would the yellow sun fit?
steps: A star's colour shows its surface temperature: blue is hottest, then white, yellow, orange and red.
Blue-white Rigel is therefore hotter than red Betelgeuse.
The yellow sun is between them.
notes.answer: Rigel is hotter. The order, hot to cool, is Rigel, the sun, Betelgeuse.

questions.prompt: Name the two forces that are balanced in a main sequence star.
questions.memo:
✓ Gravity pulling inwards (1)
✓ Outward pressure from the energy released by fusion (1)

questions.prompt: How will the sun end its life?

questions.explanation: Massive stars use their fuel much faster, so they have shorter lives.

questions.memo:

questions.prompt: Explain why scientists say that the atoms in our bodies were made in stars.
questions.memo:

✓ When stars die they scatter these elements into space, where they become part of new planets and living things (1)
